lesson.subtitle: Lesson 10 -- The Personal Essay II -- The Revision Workshop
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Stella Nassar | Lesson 10 -- The Personal Essay II
lesson.grammar_point: concision: cutting redundancy and choosing strong verbs

vocab.title: Match each word to its precise meaning
defs: using more words than are needed
to reduce something to its most essential meaning
saying the same thing twice, and therefore unnecessary
not relevant to the main subject
heavy, awkward and slow to use or read
to remove a part completely, often with care
using many words to say something that could be said simply

parts: every sentence in the middle section. She was

paras: Almost every writer I have edited arrives with the same conviction: every word in the draft is necessary. They are rarely right, and they are never entirely wrong. The words are necessary to the writer, because each one records a moment of thinking, a hesitation, a second attempt at the same idea. What they are not always necessary to is the reader.

This is why revision is so often experienced as loss. Asked to cut an essay from 800 words to 650, most students reach first for an idea. They delete a paragraph, usually the one they worked hardest on, and they feel, not unreasonably, that the essay has become smaller. A better approach reverses that instinct. Cut words first, then sentences, and whole ideas only when nothing else remains. Handled in that order, most drafts can lose a fifth of their length without losing a single thing they were trying to say.

The first cuts are almost mechanical. Redundant pairs, such as each and every or past history, can be halved without thought. Empty openings, such as it is important to note that, announce a sentence instead of writing it, and they can simply be removed. Stacked intensifiers, such as really very powerful, rarely survive a second reading, and a single precise adjective usually replaces them. Circumlocutions, such as due to the fact that or in the event that, become because and if.

Consider a single sentence from a student draft: at that particular moment in time, I made the decision to actually take a closer look at the painting in order to really understand it. It contains thirty-one words, and not one of them is wrong. Remove the circumlocution, the weak verb and the intensifiers, and the sentence becomes: at that moment, I decided to look closer, because I wanted to understand the painting. Fifteen words remain, and a reader loses nothing but the effort of reading the other sixteen. Most drafts contain dozens of sentences like the first one.

The second group requires more judgment. A weak verb carrying a noun, as in made a decision or gave consideration to, can often become a single strong verb: decided, considered. This is the reverse of a move that academic writers are taught to value, the turning of verbs into nouns, and the two lessons are not in conflict. A noun earns its place when it allows a sentence to say something a verb could not. When it merely lengthens the sentence, it is padding, however academic it sounds.

Only after these cuts should a writer consider removing sentences, and only after that, ideas. By then, the question has changed. The writer is no longer asking what can be deleted but what the essay is actually about, and that question is far easier to answer when the prose around each idea has already been cleared. Frequently, the idea that seemed essential turns out to be extraneous, and the writer can let it go without grief.

It is worth adding a warning. Concision is not brevity. A long essay can be concise if none of its words are wasted, and a short one can be padded. Nor is concision a matter of removing everything personal. The strongest revisions I have seen keep the one detail, the one rhythm, the one strange sentence that could only have come from their writer. Ruthlessness with padding is what makes that sentence visible.

choices: The shortest essay is always the best essay.
Cut wasted words first and ideas last, so that the essay loses length without losing meaning or voice.

items.situation: Cut it: "In my personal opinion, I think that..."
tips: Personal and opinion and I think all say the same thing.

items.situation: Cut it: "I made the decision to apply early."
tips: Weak verb plus noun becomes one strong verb.

items.situation: Cut it: "Due to the fact that the museum was closed, I went home."
tips: Because the museum was closed, I went home.
Due to the fact that is circumlocution for because.

items.situation: Cut it: "It is important to note that the painting is small."
tips: Delete the empty opening; if it matters, the sentence shows it.

items.situation: Cut it: "The ending was really very emotional and moving."
tips: Replace stacked intensifiers and near-synonyms with one precise word.

items.situation: Protect it: which sentence should NOT be cut? "Art has always been my passion." or "The guard warned me four times."
tips: Keep: The guard warned me four times.
Protect the sentence only you could write; cut the one anyone could.

listenings.text: Thank you for having me at the festival. I have edited magazine pieces for almost twenty years, and I want to tell you a secret about every writer I have ever worked with, including the famous ones. Every one of them believes that every word in their first draft is necessary. And every one of them is wrong, usually by about ten percent. So here is the exercise I give young writers, and I would love you to try it this week. Before you send anything to anyone, a school essay, an application, an email to a teacher, cut ten percent of it. But here is the rule. You are not allowed to remove a single idea. Only words. You will be amazed at how often you can do it. And one more thing, because people confuse these two ideas constantly. A short piece is not the same as a concise piece. A short piece simply has few words. A concise piece has no wasted ones. That means a long essay can be perfectly concise, and a short one can be full of padding.

Okay, let's talk about word limits, because I know exactly how most of you feel about them. You see a limit of six hundred and fifty words as a punishment, or at least as an obstacle standing between you and everything you want to say. I would like to persuade you that it is closer to a gift. A word limit forces you to do the hardest and most important part of writing, which is deciding what actually matters. Without a limit, you can put everything in and let the reader sort it out. With one, you have to sort it out yourself. So when your draft is too long, and it will be, cut in this order. Words first: the redundant phrases, the empty openings, the weak verbs. Then sentences. And whole ideas only at the very end, when there is truly nothing else left to remove. Most of the time, you will reach the limit before you ever get to that last step, and you will not have lost anything you care about.
